The term credits or tests demonstrated competence: an adept, a real hand. Yuanwu Keqin applies it to an interlocutor who handles an exchange, to an adept lineage teacher who frees people from entanglement, to a meeting conducted on adept terms, and to an adept Chan guest who acts as soon as a case is raised. Pang Yun exclaims it as direct praise. Xinghua Cunjiang compounds it with battle-general and demands a direct advance. Qingping Weikuang dismisses the approaching participant as not an adept. In a poetic exchange an unnamed interlocutor uses it with poet, showing that the competence belongs to the role supplied by context rather than defining only a Chan office. The corpus supports expert status, not the modern default sense author or writer. Independent later witnesses apply it to the means required of a teaching-seat master and even to Emperor Zhuangzong as an ‘adept ruler’; the competence follows the supplied role. A corpus-wide control for the ordinary verbs ‘compose,’ ‘write,’ and ‘compile,’ the ordinary noun ‘author,’ and the compound ‘adept poet’ found author/composer grammar named by other words, while the headword continues to predicate demonstrated capability.
Senses.Note: Ten exact witnesses across six distinct works. Occupational/author controls were actively tested; no curated line requires modern ‘author/writer’ as the bare-headword referent.

Senses.Explanation: An adept is the person judged capable of handling the live work of an encounter rather than merely repeating its vocabulary. Speakers ask whether an adept is present, praise a particular turn, or use the label ironically when the handling fails.

This interrogative asks how something is, how one will respond, or what can be said or done: “how?” Its force is often a live demand rather than a request for exposition. Baizhang Huaihai blocks throat and lips and asks how Guishan will speak; Shitou Xiqian rejects “this way” and “not this way” and asks what his student will do; Linji Yixuan asks how the present listener proposes to cultivate, realize, or adorn the person hearing the teaching. It also follows a proposed action—“what if the foot is raised?”—asks how someone understands a case, presses “ultimately, how?”, asks how a ceremonial address should be raised, or introduces “what is the final phrase?” Dialectal spellings perform the same interrogative work in the stored witnesses. The phrase supplies no answer by itself; its recurring role is to force the next move.

Senses.Explanation: How do you understand it? A recurrent public-interview question put to an individual or the whole assembly after a saying, action, quotation, or case has been raised. Linji Yixuan asks how an unnamed participant understands the four stated uses of a shout and answers the participant’s hesitation with a shout. Wufeng Ziqi asks, ‘How do you understand it?’ (你作麼生會); the unnamed respondent shouts, and Wufeng says ‘not yet’ (未在) before asking what comes after one shout or two. In a whisk case, Ganzi Xingzhe asks how a visitor understands Guishan Lingyou’s intention in raising the whisk; the offered account is rejected with ‘You had better return to Guishan’ (且歸溈山去好). Cuiyan Shouzhi says that National Teacher Huizhong and his attendant both still lacked understanding and asks, ‘How do you understand it now?’ (如今作麼生會). Yunju Shun similarly reopens the Puyan–Samantabhadra case for the assembly. The phrase demands an answer that can itself be answered, rejected, or tested in public; the texts do not define it as silent inward comprehension.

Senses.Explanation: “How do you say it?”—a direct demand for words in a recorded Zen public interview. Frozen-corpus concordance: 3680 exact hits in 334 storage files representing 330 independent works. Baizhang Huaihai asks Guishan Lingyou, “with throat and lips shut, how do you say it?” (併却咽喉唇吻，作麼生道); Baizhang then puts the same demand to Wufeng and Yunyan. Records also use it to demand “a phrase not involving the teaching framework” (不涉化門一句), “a phrase not falling into words” (不落言詮), or an answer from the respondent's own breast. In retrospective questions, it asks how a named earlier teacher spoke: “how did Jingshan say it to you?” (徑山向汝作麼生道). Zen bends an ordinary wording question into a public demand for an accountable spoken response. Direct and retrospective forms change subject and tense, not the thing being asked.

To calculate and guess; speculative reckoning. The graphs join ‘divine or forecast’ (卜) to ‘measure or estimate’ (度). The compound has 778 occurrences in 227 allowlisted storage files. Its recurrent coordinations locate the act in thinking, affective cognition, the root of thought, and mental weighing without creating additional senses. Dahui Zonggao says, in a list, ‘do not reckon under the root of thought; do not give a phrase; do not remain silent for a long time’ (不得向意根下卜度，不得下語，不得良久). His memorial inscription says, ‘Chan, Chan: do not use thinking and conjectural calculation; it does not concern written words and speech’ (禪禪不用思量卜度，非干文字語言). Yuanwu Keqin asks in the Blue Cliff Record whether the cited matter can be reckoned by affective cognition (以情識卜度得麼). Baoguo Zhao warns the assembly not to conjecture inside cognition because that becomes inverted imagining (莫向意識裏卜度，却成妄想顛倒). Shaoshan Daoxin gives the compact public-interview verdict: ‘if you conjecture, you lose body and life’ (卜度則喪身失命). Zen bends an ordinary term for divinatory estimation into a recurrent name for the mental guessing explicitly rejected at the teaching seat. Yongjue Yuanxian says that conjecturing within discriminating consciousness leaves only a vaguely perceived clod; Shending Yunwai Ze groups conjecture and discursive thought with outward seeking and self-binding. Both confirm the same act of speculative assessment.
Senses.Note: All required definition-form searches were negative for a true self-definition. Nine older-index hits in which a final person-marker follows the term do not define it. The term appears in questions, prohibitions, appraisals, verse, and later addresses. Its literal act and these observed constructions remain stable, so a single corpus-wide sense is used.

Senses.Explanation: The compound occurs 381 times in 145 allowed texts as a verdict on a person, answer, explanation, or speech, and as a verb for making such material up. A late direct naming statement criticizes assigning difficult cases to newcomers without matching the person and the case: after comparing it to fitting a square timber into a round hole and losing people's time, Jiexian says, 'To call it fabricated—is that not fitting?' (謂之杜撰，不亦宜乎). A playful assembly exchange separates the graphs as a surname and personal name: the staff says, 'My surname is Du, given name Zhuan'; asked why it is called 'fabricated,' it answers, 'If the elder did not fabricate, how could he spend all day talking about Zhang and Li?' (長老若不杜撰，如何終日與人說張說李). Dahui uses the word self-deprecatingly when he says, 'I have not read Guo Xiang's explanation or the various commentators' explanations; I only rely on my own fabrication to explain your silence' (我也不曾看郭象解并諸家注解，只據我杜撰說破爾這默然). The stock rebuke 'fabricated elder' (杜撰長老) occurs 68 times in 40 texts, often in the fuller comparison 'fabricated elders are like hemp and millet'—that is, extremely numerous (杜撰長老如麻似粟). 'Fabricated Chan fellow' (杜撰禪和) likewise appears as a verdict on a respondent, while 'fabricated conjectural talk' (杜撰臆說) names speech. These are grammatical deployments of one shared judgment; the texts do not establish a distinct sense from the proper name Du Mo, whose 18 hits refer to a person or to being silent.
Senses.Note: No corpus witness derives the headword from the person Du Mo. Those proper-name and silence occurrences were excluded rather than used to repeat an external etymology. The alternate 'bogus' is reserved for personal epithets such as 'bogus elder' or 'bogus Chan fellow'; 'fabricated' remains the broad target for speech, explanations, and claims.
